conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and check in on how you’re feeling emotionally.  

Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been coping over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we simply want to hear your honest experience so we can offer the best support possible.  

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me otherwise, and we’ll move at your pace. When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first question.  

To begin: Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft half-smile, eyes a little tired]  
“Honestly… most of the time I can still laugh if something’s really funny—like when my husband made that silly face at 3 a.m. while changing a diaper—but it feels muffled, like I have to work harder to feel it. It doesn’t come as easily as it used to.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

“Yes… I can still laugh, but it’s not the same quick, light feeling I had before the baby. It’s like I’m laughing because I know something’s funny, not because it naturally bubbles up. I guess I’d say I’ve been able to, just not as easily.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

“I try to—I’ll tell myself, ‘It’ll be nice to take the baby for a walk’ or ‘I used to love my morning coffee’—but when the moment comes, it feels kind of flat, like I’m just going through the motions. I wouldn’t say I never look forward to anything, but the excitement is definitely turned way down.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

“Sometimes, yeah… like if the baby won’t settle, I catch myself thinking maybe I missed some cue or I’m not doing the right thing. It’s not every time, and I usually talk myself out of it, but the thought still pops up that maybe I should’ve figured it out better.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

“Mostly it’s about the baby—worrying if his breathing sounds normal or if I’m burping him right—but every now and then I’ll feel tense and can’t really point to a reason. It’s like a low buzz of worry sitting in the background even when everything looks fine.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

“A couple of times I’ve been feeding him in the middle of the night and suddenly my heart starts racing and I feel shaky, even though nothing’s wrong. It passes pretty quickly, but it’s unsettling—like my body’s sounding an alarm I didn’t ask for.”
Things have been getting on top of me

“Yeah, some days it feels like the to-do list keeps growing faster than I can tick things off. I’ll finally get him down for a nap and realize I haven’t eaten or showered, and the dishes are still piled up. I manage—mostly—but I end those days feeling pretty drained, like I’m just treading water.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

“Not exactly unhappy—more like my mind won’t settle. I’ll lie down after a night feeding and start replaying everything: Did I sterilize the bottles right? Is he gaining enough weight? It’s not every night, maybe three or four times this week, but when it happens I stare at the ceiling for ages before I drift off.”
I have felt sad or miserable

“I do get waves of sadness—usually when I’m alone with the baby in the late afternoon. It’s not all day, and I wouldn’t call it miserable exactly, but I’ll suddenly feel like I could cry for no clear reason. It lifts after a while, maybe when my husband comes home, but it keeps catching me off-guard.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

“I haven’t broken down in tears or anything… I got a little watery-eyed one evening when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt stuck in the chair, but it didn’t turn into real crying. Mostly I just feel kind of heavy or teary, not actually sobbing.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
“No—never. I couldn’t. I want to be here for my baby, and the thought of hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind at all.”

You've shared that the joy you once felt arrives only faintly now: laughter feels forced, outings seem flat, and waves of <sym>sadness</sym> catch you off-guard in the late afternoon. While you can still meet your baby's needs, you describe a constant <sym>background anxiety</sym>, occasional <sym>panic sensations</sym>, and nights spent replaying every detail of his care. It's clear you're working incredibly hard to stay afloat and be the mother you want to be, yet you often end the day feeling drained and overwhelmed.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes diminished anticipation and emotional flattening, consistent with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient clearly describes occasional self-blame that fits "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>The mother describes both baby-specific worries and a persistent background anxiety without clear triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic symptoms (racing heart, shakiness) occurring multiple times during routine night feeds, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She describes frequent overwhelm and exhaustion but still managing, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>She experiences frequent, unpredictable waves of sadness nearly daily, aligning with "Yes, quite often" even though she avoids the word "miserable".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 15 places you above the EPDS cutoff (≥14) that signals probable <med>postpartum depression</med> and warrants prompt evaluation. You endorsed <sym>diminished enjoyment</sym> and <sym>blunted laughter</sym> (Q1-2), repeated <sym>self-reproach</sym> over infant care (Q3), persistent background <sym>anxiety</sym> and nocturnal <sym>panic symptoms</sym> (Q4-5), frequent <sym>overwhelm</sym> (Q6), several nights of <sym>sleep disruption</sym> from racing thoughts (Q7), and near-daily <sym>sad mood</sym> (Q8). These symptoms map onto core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood, loss of interest, fatigue, worthlessness, and concentration disturbance; anxiety symptoms commonly overlap. You denied self-harm thoughts (Q10=0), so immediate safety concerns are low, but severity still requires urgent follow-up. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next week to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments for <med>postpartum depression</med> such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, and antidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding if needed
3. Schedule a repeat EPDS in two weeks to track changes after starting interventions
4. Share workload: invite partner or family to handle one night feeding or household task so you can obtain a 4-hour stretch of sleep
5. Practice 5-minute grounding exercises (deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation) when <sym>anxiety</sym> or <sym>panic sensations</sym> arise
6. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep, and anxiety episodes to review with your clinician
7. Maintain nutrition and hydration by setting phone reminders for meals and keeping water within reach during feeds
8. Identify local <med>postpartum support groups</med> or online communities for encouragement and practical tips
9. Plan pleasurable micro-activities (10-minute walk with music, video call with a friend) daily to counter <sym>anhedonia</sym>
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS Interview

Symptoms / concerns endorsed  
- Reduced ability to experience pleasure or laughter (Q1, Q2)  
- Intermittent tearfulness and “waves of sadness” (Q8, Q9)  
- Sleep-onset difficulty 3–4 nights/week related to racing thoughts (Q7)  
- Unwarranted self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Background, sometimes unprovoked, anxiety; two nocturnal episodes of racing heart/shakiness (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed and “drained” by daily tasks (Q6)  

Patterns noted  
Mild-to-moderate anhedonia, situational tearfulness, and physiologic anxiety without full panic; no avoidance of infant care; no self-harm ideation (Q10 denied).

Screening significance  
Findings consistent with possible postpartum depression and/or generalized anxiety; no current safety concerns. Recommend routine follow-up and formal clinical assessment for diagnostic clarification and intervention planning.
